rv.q: "Promises, Promises" is a candy-flavored ride that more than delivers on its title.

The show doesn’t play anywhere near as well as it once did; changes have been made to the material that turn out to be ill-advised — changing the emphasis, slowing the momentum, and throwing sand into the gears of Simon’s laugh machine.

It seems we have "Mad Men" to thank for the buoyant new production of "Promises, Promises," receiving its first Broadway revival since its premiere more than 40 years ago. This musical adaptation of Billy Wilder’s classic film "The Apartment" has clearly tapped into the ’60s era nostalgia so vividly rendered by the AMC television series.
The musical always has been a tired businessman's kind of show even as it spoofs the sexism so prevalent in the day.
“Promises, Promises” doesn’t exactly fulfill them, but its compensations are so vivid that it’s impossible to walk away feeling entirely cheated.
No matter how high they jump or how much body heat they expend, they never manage to push the evening’s temperature much above lukewarm.
Saving their redeeming presences, 'Promises, Promises' is slick, pointless and forgettable.

The actor is nimble, funny, likable, and much more asexually wholesome than one might expect given that his character has agreed to allow his philandering bosses to use his midtown apartment for trysts in hopes of securing a promotion.
The new production, directed and choreographed by Rob Ashford, is stylish and handsome, but only occasionally memorable.
Problems, like promises, abound. First, adultery seems very nearly to have exhausted its talent to titillate.
Still, after an uneven and at times tiresome two and a half hours, you'll leave Promises unfulfilled.
Sean Hayes, so busy knowing he's funny that you never believe the hero's suffering, and Kristin Chenoweth, the Teflon actress, to whom no emotion ever sticks.
A 1997. Encores! concert managed to unearth charms in the problematic material. No such miracle is occurring at the Broadway Theatre.
The plot wasn't appetizing when the show – based on Billy Wilder's cynical film "The Apartment" – opened in 1968, and now it's downright distasteful.
An immensely appealing Sean Hayes is terrific in a nice guy hero role created by Jerry Orbach.
Sean Hayes is thoroughly adorable as Chuck Baxter, displaying great rapport with the audience and genuine comedic charm.
But it all went wrong. Not hold-your-head-in-your-hands-and-moan wrong, but — even worse — deep into that melancholy Neverland of what might have been.

cn.t: This revival of the 1968 musical delivers Bacharach's fizzy, period-defining score but struggles with Simon's dated book and uneven casting, resulting in a stylish yet only occasionally memorable production.

vs.sum: The Broadway Theatre's vast size (1,761 seats) and exceptional depth mean rear orchestra and balcony seats are very far from the stage, making it best suited to large-scale spectacle productions. The Renaissance-inspired interior is grand, though comfort is below average with tight seating.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
